section.title: The Fall of Nineveh
section.sectionRationale: The oracle turns from announcement to eyewitness vision. Nahum watches, as though standing on the walls, the attack that will end Nineveh: the scarlet-clad assault, the river gates bursting, the plunder, the panic, and the lion's den left empty. It closes with the LORD Himself declaring war on the city.
section.thesis: Nineveh, the lion that filled its den with the torn flesh of the nations, is besieged, emptied, and undone, because the LORD of Hosts has set Himself against her.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the call to defend and the LORD restoring Jacob; the dazzling, chaotic assault; the city plundered and hearts melting; and the lion's empty den under God's declared war.

units.label: The attacker comes, the LORD restores
units.note: guard the fortress, for God will restore Jacob

verses.text: One who {{puwts|scatters}} advances against you, O Nineveh. Guard the fortress! Watch the road! Brace yourselves! Summon all your strength!
For the LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob like the splendor of Israel, though destroyers have laid them waste and ruined the branches of their vine.

units.label: The dazzling, chaotic assault
units.note: chariots like torches, the river gates opened

verses.text: The shields of his mighty men are red; the valiant warriors are dressed in scarlet. The fittings of the chariots flash like fire on the day they are prepared, and the spears of cypress have been brandished.
The chariots dash through the streets; they rush around the plazas, appearing like torches, darting about like lightning.
He summons his nobles; they stumble as they advance. They race to its wall; the protective shield is set in place.
The river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses.

units.label: The city plundered, hearts melting
units.note: plunder the silver, plunder the gold

verses.text: It is decreed that the city be exiled and carried away; her maidservants moan like doves, and beat upon their breasts.
Nineveh has been like a pool of water throughout her days, but now it is draining away. “Stop! Stop!” they cry, but no one turns back.
“Plunder the silver! Plunder the gold!” There is no end to the treasure, an abundance of every precious thing.
She is {{buqah|emptied}}! Yes, she is desolate and laid waste! Hearts melt, knees knock, bodies tremble, and every face grows pale!

units.label: The lion's empty den, and God against her
units.note: the LORD of Hosts declares war

verses.text: Where is the {{ariy|lions'}} lair or the feeding ground of the young lions, where the lion and lioness prowled with their cubs, with nothing to frighten them away?
The lion mauled enough for its cubs and strangled prey for the lioness. It filled its dens with the kill, and its lairs with mauled prey.

“Behold, I am {{hinneni|against you}},” declares the LORD of {{tsava|Hosts}}. “I will reduce your chariots to cinders, and the sword will devour your young lions. I will cut off your prey from the earth, and the voices of your messengers will no longer be heard.”

puwts.gloss: To scatter, disperse, or shatter. Nahum calls the coming attacker the one who scatters, the very fate Assyria had inflicted on countless peoples now turned back upon her. The empire that scattered the nations will itself be scattered.

buqah.gloss: Emptiness, desolation. In verse 10 Nahum stacks three similar-sounding Hebrew words together, buqah, mebuqah, mebullaqah, so the very sound of the line thuds like a hammer of ruin. English cannot fully carry the effect: she is emptied, desolate, and laid waste.

ariy.gloss: A lion. Assyria proudly used the lion as its royal symbol, and its palaces were lined with lion hunts. Nahum turns the image against them: the lion that filled its den with torn prey now finds its lair empty, for a greater power has come.

hinneni.gloss: Behold, here I am, or I am against you. When God says hinneni followed by against you, it is the language of a warrior turning to face an enemy. There is no more chilling word for Nineveh than to hear the LORD Himself declare that He now stands against her.

tsava.gloss: Hosts or armies. The title LORD of Hosts names God as commander of the armies of heaven, the marshaled powers of the universe. Against such a general Nineveh's chariots and warriors are nothing.

basic.context: Nineveh was the fortified capital of Assyria, a city that had terrorized the nations for generations. In this chapter Nahum describes its fall as if he were watching it happen: an army storming in, the river gates giving way, the palace collapsing, the treasures looted, and the people in panic. The great lion's den is left empty.
basic.hermeneutics: This is vivid prophetic poetry describing a real event, the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC. It is not a manual for warfare; it is a picture of what happens when God finally moves against entrenched evil. The turning point is verse 13: the reason the city falls is that God says, I am against you.
basic.originalLanguages: The attacker is the one who scatters, puwts, the same thing Assyria did to others. Verse 10 hammers out three near-identical Hebrew words for emptiness. The lion, ariy, was Assyria's proud emblem, now mocked. And the decisive words are hinneni, I am against you, spoken by the LORD of Hosts, tsava, the commander of heaven's armies.
basic.typology: Nineveh, the lion filling its den with torn prey, pictures every violent power that devours the weak. Its sudden emptying foreshadows the final overthrow of every proud kingdom set against God, and the LORD of Hosts declaring war anticipates Christ's certain victory over all His enemies.
basic.christ: The words I am against you are terrifying, and they show why the gospel is such good news. In Christ, God is no longer against those who trust Him but for them. The same LORD of Hosts who marched against Nineveh marched to the cross and rose in triumph, and He will one day empty every violent stronghold for good.
basic.god: We learn that God repays violence with justice, that no fortress or wealth can save a city He opposes, and that human pride is no match for the LORD of Hosts. Yet even here mercy shines: He is restoring the splendor of His own people, verse 2.
basic.crossReferences: Zephaniah 2 also foretells Nineveh's ruin. Proverbs 16 warns that pride goes before destruction. And the assurance that God is against His enemies but restores His people points to Romans 8, that if God is for us, no one can stand against us.
basic.oneStory: The fall of the great predator city is a chapter in the long story of God bringing down every power that devours His people. It anticipates the day when Babylon the great, the last Nineveh, falls forever and the Lamb who was slain reigns in peace.

context.literary:
Nahum 2 is built like a film in three reels. Verse 1 is a single scene of mocking commands and the verse that follows, verse 2, is a quick cut to Judah's restoration. Verses 3 to 10 are the assault itself: the glitter of the attackers in verses 3 and 4, the defenders' scramble in verse 5, the breach in verse 6, the exile and the moaning in verse 7, the draining of the city and the plunder in verses 8 and 9, and the empty ruin in verse 10. Verses 11 to 13 then pull back and ask a question, 'Where is the lions' lair?', and answer it with the divine declaration of verse 13.

The poem's own sound carries meaning. Short clipped clauses mimic rushing chariots, and the sudden juxtapositions leave the reader a little disoriented, as a person would be inside a besieged city. The four commands of verse 1, 'Guard the fortress! Watch the road! Brace yourselves! Summon all your strength!', are sarcasm, since the Hebrew pairs of words in the first command play on each other, a kind of 'guard the guarding.' The defenders are told to do everything, and nothing will help.

The interruption of verse 2 is also deliberate. In the middle of the siege we are told that the LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob. It is the poem's first look at the reason for the assault: the destroyer of Jacob is being destroyed. The lion passage at the end works the other way, collecting the whole poem into one image of a predator whose den is bare. The chapter begins with a command to a city and ends with the LORD declaring, 'Behold, I am against you.' Everything in between is the working out of that sentence.
context.historical:
Nineveh sat on the east bank of the Tigris, the royal city of Assyria after Sennacherib made it his capital and ringed it with walls and moats. It fell in 612 BC after a siege by the Babylonians under Nabopolassar and the Medes, and a Babylonian chronicle records the event. Nahum wrote decades earlier, when the empire's strength seemed beyond challenge, so the oracle is a prediction and not a report.

The lion imagery has a documented background. Assyrian palaces were decorated with reliefs of the king hunting and killing lions, an image of royal power, and Assyria's kings spoke of themselves as devourers of the nations. Isaiah 10:13 and 14 records the boast, 'I have removed the boundaries of nations and plundered their treasures.' The prophet turns the royal emblem against the empire. The lions' lair of verses 11 and 12 is the city itself, where the spoil of the nations was brought in and stored.

The scene of plunder also fits what Nineveh actually was. Silver and gold taken from conquered peoples filled its palaces, and verse 9 says there is no end to the treasure. The treasure that the Assyrians took through terror is now taken from them. Habakkuk 2:8 states the principle: because you have plundered many nations, the remnant of the people will plunder you.

The mention of messengers in verse 13 echoes the Assyrian practice of sending envoys to threaten other kings. The Rabshakeh stood outside Jerusalem and shouted in Hebrew, 'Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria!' 2 Kings 18:28. That voice, the verse says, will not be heard again. The reference to exile in verse 7 recalls that Assyria had itself deported the peoples it conquered, such as the northern tribes in 2 Kings 15:29.
context.canonical:
Nahum 2 belongs to a line of oracles against Assyria that begins with Isaiah, who called it the rod of God's anger and then announced the rod's breaking, Isaiah 10:5 to 15, and who said that a destroyer will be destroyed, Isaiah 33:1. Zephaniah 2:13 to 15 foretells Nineveh's end in similar terms and quotes her boast, 'I am it, and there is none besides me.' Jonah comes first in the canon of the Twelve and shows the other side of the same city: when Nineveh repented, God relented, Jonah 3:10.

The phrase 'I am against you' is one of the prophets' formulas of war. It is used against Jerusalem in Ezekiel 5:8, against Tyre in Ezekiel 26:3, against Babylon in Jeremiah 50:31 and repeated against Nineveh in Nahum 3:5. A reader who knows the formula hears that Nineveh has been placed among the cities that God Himself has taken on.

The lions of Nahum 2 also belong to a wider biblical theme. Rulers who devour the weak are lions: Proverbs 28:15 compares a wicked ruler over a helpless people to a roaring lion, and Ezekiel 19 laments the princes as young lions who learned to tear their prey. At the other end of the canon, Genesis 49:9 gives Judah a lion's image and Revelation 5:5 calls Christ the Lion of the tribe of Judah. Nineveh's fall prefigures the fall of Babylon in Revelation 18, the last city of this kind, whose judgment comes in a single hour, Revelation 18:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Nahum wants a frightened people to see what the siege looks like from God's side. A Judean who heard of Assyria's armies could imagine only the terror. The prophet gives them the same pictures of chariots, torches and falling walls, but turned around, so that the attackers are marching against Nineveh and the city that terrorised everyone else is now the one gripped by panic. The poem is told in the present tense so that it feels as certain as news.

He also wants to explain why. A reader might take the fall of a city as politics: the Medes and Babylonians were strong, and Assyria had grown weak. The poem refuses that explanation. The deepest reason is given in verse 13: 'Behold, I am against you,' declares the LORD of Hosts. The armies in verses 3 and 4 are real, but they are the visible edge of a decision made in heaven. Nahum wants Judah to understand that history is not shaped by empires alone.

There is a pastoral purpose in the short verse 2 as well. Judah is told that her ruin is not final. The one who has laid waste the branches of the vine is being laid waste, and the splendor of Jacob will be restored. The prophet means the people to hear in the middle of the battle a promise addressed to them: God has not forgotten the ruined vine, and the fall of the oppressor is for the sake of His people.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter describes a coming event in poetry. It does not teach tactics of siege or give permission to plunder, and the plunder of verse 9 is a record of what will happen to a proud city, not a command. Nor should the vivid images of terror be taken as a model for how God's people should treat their enemies. The commands of verse 1 are sarcastic, spoken to the city and not to believers.

The chapter does teach by example how to read power. Where a city, a regime or an economic system looks unassailable, the passage supplies a corrective: the LORD of Hosts is not impressed. The believer is not asked to predict which empire will fall next or to read the news as a code. The principle is the one in Proverbs 16:18, that pride goes before destruction, applied to a specific case.

The passage also invites a response of trust. Verse 2 is a promise made to people who had no way of seeing how it would happen. Those who live under pressure are not told when relief will come, but they are told whose decision it is. The abiding application is to hold two things together: to take seriously the danger of powers that devour, and to refuse to be intimidated by them.

debates.question: Does verse 6, the river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses, refer to a literal flood?

views.label: A literal river breach
views.case: Ancient tradition and the geography of Nineveh, set among rivers, suggest the Khoser or Tigris waters were used or rose to break the walls, matching the collapse of the palace; the vision reads as reportage of the actual siege. The sounds of the poem also support it: the pool that drains in verse 8 fits a city whose water defences have failed. The same picture was promised in 1:8, an overwhelming flood.

views.label: Vivid siege imagery
views.case: Others take the river gates more figuratively for the city's defenses giving way under assault, in keeping with the poem's rapid, impressionistic style. A prophecy written decades before the event is less likely to describe a particular engineering detail, and the phrase can simply mean that the places thought safest are the first to open.

debates.bearing: Whether the flood was literal or a striking image, the point is the same: Nineveh's defenses fail utterly, because the true besieger is the LORD of Hosts declaring war on the city.

debates.question: Whose army fills the streets in verses 3 and 4?

views.label: The attackers
views.case: The scarlet shields and crimson clothing match what Scripture says of the Babylonians, whose soldiers were painted in vermilion, Ezekiel 23:14. The 'one who scatters' of verse 1 is the subject, and the verses describe his army as it prepares and enters. On this reading the chariots race through Nineveh's streets because they have broken in.

views.label: The defenders
views.case: Verse 5 speaks of the nobles who stumble as they race to the wall, and some read verses 3 and 4 in the same vein, as the city's own chariots dashing through the plazas in a futile defence. Since the Hebrew does not name the subject, the poem could be showing the city's flurry of activity.

views.label: Deliberately both
views.case: A few interpreters suggest that the poem blurs the two on purpose. The reader sees only flashing metal and a dust of motion, and cannot tell which side is which, because from Nineveh's point of view it makes no difference.

debates.bearing: The first view has the strongest support from the colour language, but the passage's meaning does not hang on the answer. In every reading, the armies move, the city cannot hold, and God is behind it.

debates.question: What does verse 7 say, 'It is decreed that the city be exiled'?

views.label: A decree or settled fate
views.case: The BSB takes the first Hebrew word as a verb meaning something has been fixed or decreed. The sense is that the exile of the city has been determined, which fits the sovereign tone of the whole chapter.

views.label: A proper name, Huzzab
views.case: Some translations leave the word untranslated as 'Huzzab,' a name, and take it as the queen of Nineveh, a goddess, or a poetic name for the city, so that 'Huzzab is led away captive.' The difficulty is that no such name is otherwise known, so the reading depends on a guess.

debates.bearing: The decree reading is simpler, and the second view is a reminder of how uncertain some Hebrew words are. Either way the verse shows the people of the city led away like the peoples Assyria once deported, and the maidservants moaning like doves.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse is a string of sarcastic commands: 'Guard the fortress! Watch the road! Brace yourselves! Summon all your strength!' The first command in Hebrew sets two forms of the same root side by side, natsor metsurah, so that it is almost 'guard the guard post.' The third, which the BSB footnote gives literally as 'Strengthen your loins,' uses the picture of tightening the waist for action. In verse 10 the same part of the body returns, for the Hebrew says there is anguish in all loins. The commanded strengthening of verse 1 is answered by the collapse of verse 10. The second command, 'Watch the road,' uses the verb tsafah, to look out, the verb of the watchman in Habakkuk 2:1.

Verse 2 uses a Hebrew pair of words that sound like each other. The destroyers have 'laid waste' Jacob, from the root baqaq, to empty, and the same root appears in verse 10 in the cry that Nineveh is emptied, in a run of three near-rhyming words. The empire that emptied Israel is emptied by the same word. Just before this, God 'will restore the splendor of Jacob,' and the Hebrew word for splendor, gaon, is usually the word for pride. Amos 6:8 has God saying He abhors the gaon of Jacob, and Proverbs 16:18 uses it of the pride that goes before destruction. In Nahum it turns positive: what was pride in Jacob is to be transformed into glory.

Verse 3 says the 'shields' are red and the warriors 'scarlet,' and the BSB footnote at verse 3 notes that the Hebrew of the spears of cypress can also be read as pine, juniper or fir, and that the Greek and Syriac read the clause differently. Such footnotes warn against reading too much into any single detail.

In verse 6 the palace 'collapses,' and the word is a verb meaning to melt or dissolve, the same root as the hills melting in 1:5. The Hebrew word for palace is heikal, the word also used for the LORD's temple. The word for the river gates is plural, 'the gates of the rivers,' suggesting more than one channel.

In verse 7 the moaning women 'beat upon their breasts.' The verb comes from the root for a tambourine, so that they are literally drumming on their hearts. Women had once taken up tambourines to celebrate a deliverance, Exodus 15:20 and Psalm 68:25. Here the instrument is their own chest.

In verse 9 the order to 'Plunder' repeats, and the word for treasure, 'every precious thing,' comes from the root chamad, to desire, the root in 'You shall not covet,' Exodus 20:17. What Assyria desired and seized is now desired and seized from it.

Verses 11 and 12 use more than one Hebrew word for lion: the lion, the lioness, the young lion and the cub. Job 4:10 and 11 shows how rich the vocabulary is, and Nahum draws on several words at once so that the whole family appears. The lair is the place where they lie down 'with nothing to frighten them away,' and the sentence of verse 13 is that the sword will 'devour' the young lions, using the verb for eating. The eater is eaten.

Verse 13 opens with hineni elayikh, 'Behold, I am against you,' with the declaration 'declares the LORD of Hosts,' the same word formula the prophets use of God's own speech. The last clause is that the voice of your messengers will no longer be heard. The word for messengers is mal'akh, the envoy, and it is set deliberately against the mevasser of 1:15, the herald on the mountains. One messenger is silenced and the other is heard.

typology.type: The devouring lion and the Lion of Judah, Nahum 2:11 to 13
typology.fulfillment: Nineveh is the lion that fills its den with the kill, and the sword devours its young lions. The New Testament names the greater predator behind such powers: 'Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour,' 1 Peter 5:8. Against him stands the true Lion, 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah' who 'has triumphed,' Revelation 5:5, from Jacob's blessing of Judah in Genesis 49:9. The strange turn is that John looks and sees 'a Lamb who appeared to have been slain,' Revelation 5:6. The Lion triumphs as the Lamb. The type falls short because Nineveh's lion was one more earthly tyrant, whereas the enemy behind it is a spiritual one cast down by Christ, John 12:31.

typology.type: Nineveh as the first Babylon, Nahum 2:6 to 10
typology.fulfillment: The pattern of a proud, rich city thrown down in a day is carried through the prophets and reaches its end in Revelation 18. There the great city of Babylon is cried over, 'In a single hour your judgment has come,' Revelation 18:10, and a mighty angel casts a stone like a great millstone into the sea with the words, 'With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again,' Revelation 18:21. The correspondences are the plunder, the sudden collapse, and the silence that follows. The type is more local than its fulfilment: Nineveh was a particular city, but Babylon in Revelation stands for every power that sets itself up against God.

typology.type: The ruined vine and the true Vine, Nahum 2:2
typology.fulfillment: God promises to restore 'the splendor of Jacob' though destroyers have 'ruined the branches of their vine.' Israel was often pictured as a vine. Psalm 80:8 to 16 says God uprooted a vine from Egypt and planted it, and the prayer asks Him to attend to it after it was cut down and burned. Isaiah 5:7 says the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel. Jesus says, 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1, taking the role Israel did not fulfil. The correspondence is that a ruined vine is restored by God's own action. The type falls short because the vine of the Old Testament produced bad fruit, and Christ brings forth the fruit that was looked for.

typology.type: The splendor restored to Jacob, Nahum 2:2
typology.fulfillment: The restoration of Jacob's splendor looks beyond the end of Assyria to the rebuilding of what God's people had lost. Amos 9:11 promised to restore the fallen tent of David, and in Acts 15:16 and 17 James says that this promise is being fulfilled as Gentiles seek the Lord. At the end, the holy city comes down from heaven 'shining with the glory of God,' Revelation 21:11. The escalation is that the glory is no longer a regional splendor of a single nation, but the glory of God shared by people from every nation. The type is limited in that Judah's recovery was partial and temporary, and the fulfilment is to be permanent.

study.christ:
Nahum 2 leads to Christ most clearly by the contrast of its two sentences about God's posture. Verse 13 says, 'Behold, I am against you,' declares the LORD of Hosts. Verse 2 has said that the LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob. God is against the destroyer and for the destroyed, and the chapter holds the two sentences in one breath. Paul takes the second as the confession of the gospel: 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' Romans 8:31. The 'I am against you' that Nahum pronounces on Nineveh is the posture the Bible says God holds toward sin and toward the powers that enslave. In Christ it is the posture God holds toward sin and the enemies of His people, and it is why the people can say He is for them.

The lion image also leads to Christ. Revelation 5:5 tells the weeping John that 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed.' The empire that made itself a lion is ended by the sword, but the true Lion triumphs by being slain, so John turns and sees a Lamb who appeared to have been slain. The roaring predator of 1 Peter 5:8 is, according to Jesus, already judged: 'Now judgment is upon this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out,' John 12:31, and 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven,' Luke 10:18. Colossians 2:15 says that at the cross He 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and made 'a public spectacle of them.' Hebrews 2:14 says He shared our humanity to destroy him who holds the power of death. Nineveh's fall is a small sign of that larger defeat.

The passage also leads to Christ through the figure of the vine. Judah's ruined vine in verse 2 gives way in the Gospel of John to the one who says, 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1. What Israel failed to be, He is, and those who belong to Him are the branches that bear fruit. The restoration of Jacob's splendor is, in the end, the gathering of people in Him.

There is a sobering side too. The voice of Nineveh's messengers will be heard no more, while the feet of the herald of 1:15 are still on the mountains. Jesus' own message is the one that is not silenced, and He sends it out to every nation, Matthew 28:19. Those who are 'against' Him will find that His kingdom is not shaken, Hebrews 12:28.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Nahum 2 does not name the Messiah, and the details of the scarlet shields and the river gates are not coded predictions of Christ. The passage leads to Him through its main claim, that God breaks the powers that devour His people and restores the people, and through the images the New Testament takes up: the lion, the vine, the fallen city. The fall of Nineveh is a signpost on the road to the cross, where the greatest of all the enemies was defeated.
study.god:
Nahum 2 shows a God who is at work through events that look wholly human. The armies that march, the river that breaks the gate, the plunderers who strip the palace are all real and all explainable, and yet verse 13 says the cause is the LORD of Hosts. The Hebrew name tsevaot, 'of Hosts,' presents Him as the commander of every army, including the armies that are His instruments. This is the doctrine of providence at its starkest: God governs the movement of nations without being a participant in their politics.

He is opposed to what devours. The chapter's central image is of a predator that has gorged on what is not its own, and God's declaration is the end of that business. It shows that His justice is not abstract but matched to what has been done. Nineveh filled its dens with prey, and its prey is cut off. The word of judgment is a direct answer to the lives of the people who were hurt, and it tells us that God notices what is taken from the weak.

He is not capricious. Nahum 3:19, in the next chapter, will say that no one has escaped Nineveh's cruelty, and Jonah showed that He had once held back from destroying the city when it repented. So the fall in Nahum 2 is not the destruction of a city that never had a chance. God was patient, Nineveh turned back to violence, and the sentence comes at last. His judgment follows His patience, not the other way round.

He is faithful to His people. The sudden verse 2 shows that even when the battle is focused on another city, God has Judah in mind. 'The LORD will restore the splendor of Jacob like the splendor of Israel.' The word for pride has turned to splendor; what was lost is restored. The God who judges the destroyer is the God who is committed to the ruined vine, and the two are one commitment.

He is also the God of whom the powerful have reason to be afraid. The hearts that melt and the knees that knock in verse 10 are a sign of what it is to meet Him without refuge. This is the reverse of the confidence of 1:7. Proverbs 21:30 says there is no wisdom, no understanding and no counsel that can prevail against the LORD.

For worship, the chapter calls for a sober kind of joy. It is not the joy of the plunderers but the joy of a people who are told that their oppressor is not eternal. It also calls for humility, since Nineveh's pride is a warning to every nation, and every heart, that rests on its own walls. And it directs prayer: 'Where is the lions' lair?' is the question those who suffer under tyranny may ask with confidence, because He has already answered it.

crossReferences.note: The overture promised an overwhelming flood that would make an end of Nineveh. Chapter 2 delivers the picture with the river gates thrown open and the palace dissolving, so the hymn and the battle poem belong together. The hymn gave the cause and the battle poem shows the effect.

God repeats the declaration, 'Behold, I am against you,' in the next chapter. It frames the two battle poems with the same sentence. The repetition tells us that the decisive thing about Nineveh's end is God's settled position toward it, not the strength of its enemies.

God says He will punish the king of Assyria for the fruit of his arrogant heart, and asks whether an axe raises itself above the one who swings it. The Assyrian boast of plundering the nations and the divine response set the background for Nahum 2. The empire was an instrument that forgot who held it.

Because Assyria plundered many nations, the remnant of the people will plunder it. The principle behind the plunder of Nahum 2:9 is that violence returns on those who practise it. Habakkuk speaks of Babylon, but the moral law is the same, and Nahum's treasure scene is a case of it.

Another prophetic word on Nineveh's end. God will make the city a desolation, a resting place for beasts, and it quotes the boast, 'I am it, and there is none besides me.' It agrees with Nahum on the cause and adds the voice of pride that the fall answers.

A lament in which Israel's princes are young lions who learn to tear their prey and devour men and are then trapped and led away. It shows that the lion image was used of rulers who devour, and that the end of such a lion is a cage and a silenced roar, as in Nahum 2:13.

The earlier word to the same city. Nineveh heard Jonah's warning, fasted and turned from violence, and God relented. Nahum 2 follows the later generation that went back to violence. The two texts show that the fall was not the first word God spoke to Nineveh but the last.

Christ is the Lion of the tribe of Judah who has triumphed, and when John looks he sees a Lamb who appeared to have been slain. The image of the lion is taken from the enemies of God's people and given to the one who defeats them, by sacrifice and not by devouring.

A mighty angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea and says Babylon will be cast down with such violence and never be seen again. The fall of Nineveh is the Old Testament model for the final fall of the city that stands against God, and the finality of Nahum's emptied city is here repeated.

Paul asks, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' The statement answers Nahum 2:13 from the other side. The God who is against Nineveh is for His people, and this is the settled posture of the God of the Bible toward those who trust Him.

Jesus says, 'I am the true vine.' Nahum 2:2 speaks of destroyers who ruined the branches of Israel's vine, and Psalm 80 and Isaiah 5 describe the vine that failed to bear what God looked for. Jesus takes up that image as the one in whom the vine is fruitful and by whom ruined branches are restored.

study.oneStory:
Nahum 2 stands in the long line of stories where a city built on violence is brought down. Cain built a city, Babel a tower, Egypt a house of bondage, and the Bible keeps returning to them as pictures of human power organised against God. The big cities of the Old Testament each have their moment: Egypt at the Red Sea, Assyria in Nahum, Babylon in Isaiah and Jeremiah. Nineveh is one chapter in a story of the end of oppressors.

The chapter also puts into view a second line, that of the ruined vine. Israel is God's vine in Psalm 80 and Isaiah 5, planted in good ground and meant to bear fruit. It is trampled by those who should have served it, and God promises to restore it. Nahum 2:2 is one of the quietest of those promises, tucked inside a battle scene. The destroyer's fall is for the sake of the vine.

The passage sits near the middle of the prophets' answer to the question 'How long?' It is an answer within history, a fall that occurred in 612 BC. But Babylon follows, and Persia, Greece and Rome after, and the same question has to be asked again. Each fall is a down payment on the final one, and the story trains its readers to read every collapse of an arrogant power as a sign.

It arrives at the cross, where the decisive defeat of the enemy behind all empires is won. The Lion of Judah triumphs as a Lamb, and the ruler of this world is cast out, John 12:31. The church lives between this defeat and its full display, as Nineveh's neighbours lived between the prophecy and the fall. Revelation 18 shows the last Babylon thrown down, and the city of God, the new Jerusalem, descends with the glory of God, Revelation 21:10 and 11.

In the new creation there are no more lions' lairs, because there is no more prey. Isaiah 11:6 pictures the wolf dwelling with the lamb, and the earth is filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea, Habakkuk 2:14. The splendor of Jacob is restored in a people from every nation, and the promise of verse 2 is shown to have been kept.

quiz.q: According to verse 13, why does Nineveh ultimately fall?

options.text: Because the LORD of Hosts declares, Behold, I am against you.
options.note: The true cause is God Himself setting His armies against the city.

options.text: Only because its enemies happened to be militarily stronger.
options.note: Enemies do attack, but the text names God as the decisive cause.

options.text: Because its walls were poorly built.
options.note: Nineveh was heavily fortified; the issue is that God opposed her.

options.text: By pure chance, with no cause given.
options.note: Nahum gives a clear cause: God has set Himself against her.

quiz.q: What is the point of the lion imagery in verses 11-12?

options.text: Assyria's own royal symbol is turned against it; the predator's den is now empty.
options.note: The lion that filled its den with torn prey is mocked as its lair falls empty.

options.text: It shows that lions literally lived in the city.
options.note: The lion is a symbol of Assyria's violence and royalty, not a zoo.

options.text: It recalls Assyria's ferocity as a predator, now in order to announce its ruin.
options.note: Right that the lion evokes Assyria's ferocity, but the thrust is judgment: the den is empty.

options.text: It has no connection to Assyria at all.
options.note: The lion was Assyria's proud emblem, deliberately used here.

quiz.q: How does the word about God restoring Jacob, verse 2, fit into this chapter of judgment?

options.text: God's judgment on the oppressor and His mercy to His people flow from one righteous heart.
options.note: The fall of Nineveh is the flip side of the restoration of God's people.

options.text: It is out of place and unrelated to the rest.
options.note: It is deliberately woven in to show the purpose behind the judgment.

options.text: It shows God is acting for His people even while He judges Nineveh.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it specifically ties Nineveh's fall to His people's restoration.

options.text: It shows God has given up on His people.
options.note: The verse promises restoration, the opposite of abandonment.

quiz.q: Why does the verdict I am against you make the gospel such good news?

options.text: In Christ God is no longer against those who trust Him but for them, Romans 8:31.
options.note: The cross reverses the verdict for all who take refuge in Christ.

options.text: Because it proves God is never really against anyone.
options.note: God truly opposes evil; the gospel is that Christ bears that opposition for us.

options.text: Because Christ shields believers, though God's opposition to evil remains real.
options.note: Close: believers are shielded in Christ, who bore the wrath, which is not merely waved away.

options.text: It has no bearing on the gospel.
options.note: The reversal of God's verdict is at the very heart of the gospel.

quiz.q: What does the title LORD of Hosts emphasize in verse 13?

options.text: God commands the armies of heaven, so no chariot or fortress can stand against Him.
options.note: Hosts, tsava, names God as the supreme commander of all powers.

options.text: That God commands vast armies, though these are the hosts of heaven, not hired men.
options.note: Right that it speaks of armies, but the hosts are heaven's powers, not a human payroll.

options.text: That God is only a local deity of Judah.
options.note: The title asserts universal command, far beyond any locality.

options.text: That God is distant and uninvolved.
options.note: He is intimately and actively at war against Nineveh.

questions: Nineveh trusted its walls, its wealth, and its armies, yet none could save it. What are you tempted to trust for security that could not stand if God were against it?
The lion that devoured others found its own den empty. Where do you see the pattern that violence and pride finally consume themselves?
The most fearful words here are I am against you. How does it move you to know that in Christ God has become for you rather than against you?
In the middle of judgment God promises to restore the splendor of His people. Where do you need to trust that God is restoring what evil or loss has ruined in your life?
The LORD of Hosts commands every power in heaven and earth. How would facing this week as one whose God is that great commander change the way you meet your fears?

translationNotes.note: Brace yourselves renders a Hebrew phrase meaning literally strengthen your loins, a call to gird up for battle; the taunt is bitterly ironic, since no strength will save the city.
Spears of cypress reflects the Hebrew; some ancient versions read differently, and the wood may be pine, juniper, or fir, but the picture of massed, brandished weaponry is clear.
She is emptied, desolate, and laid waste translates three Hebrew words of almost identical sound, buqah mebuqah mebullaqah, whose hammering assonance drives home the totality of the ruin.
